prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, haloperidol or other centrally acting D2-blocking antiemetics or antipsychotics; if an antipsychotic is needed, use quetiapine or clozapine
Do not prescribe centrally acting anticholinergics (trihexyphenidyl, benztropine) in a patient with cognitive impairment (MoCA 24/30)
required_recommendations: Diagnose clinically established PD with motor fluctuations (MDS 2015): left-onset bradykinesia with rigidity and rest tremor, a documented response to levodopa of more than 50% and a limb rest tremor as two supportive criteria, no red flag; twice-monthly prochlorperazine predating the PD is not a dose and time course consistent with drug-induced parkinsonism [Postuma_2015]
Stop prochlorperazine and treat migraine-associated nausea without central D2 blockade: ondansetron (unless apomorphine is used) or domperidone where available after an ECG for the QTc

Manage the predictable end-of-dose wearing-off: shorten the levodopa dosing interval to the 2.5 hours each dose lasts (for example 25/100 mg every 2.5 hours while awake, five or six doses a day) or add entacapone with each dose, an MAO-B inhibitor or a dopamine agonist; if an agonist is used, warn about impulse control disorders and excessive daytime sleepiness and ask about them at every visit [NICE_NG71]
Refer to physiotherapy for OFF-period freezing and falls, with external cueing (visual and auditory), strategies for doorways and turning, and a home fall-risk assessment [NICE_NG71]
Increase levothyroxine for the TSH of 5.8 mIU/L (for example from 75 to 88 micrograms daily, taken on an empty stomach) and recheck TSH in 6 to 8 weeks; omeprazole can reduce its absorption

avoided_actions.rationale: The OFF periods are dose-locked motor episodes with preserved awareness, not seizures: EEG has no role
A 4-year levodopa-responsive parkinsonism with no inflammatory or infectious feature: CSF has no role
No murmur, heart failure or cardiac symptom: an echocardiogram does not inform the fluctuations
Her falls occur during freezing at doorways, not from syncope or palpitations: rhythm monitoring is not indicated
Formal autonomic testing is not part of the PD work-up; bedside orthostatic measurement suffices

differential.key_features: Aggravating factor: each prochlorperazine dose can transiently worsen her motor state, but twice-monthly use does not explain the dose-locked wearing-off documented in her diary or the 4-year asymmetric course with a sustained levodopa response
Coexists: TSH 5.8 mIU/L with free T4 0.9 ng/dL on levothyroxine; contributes to fatigue and slowing, not the cause of the rest tremor, asymmetry or OFF periods

Sustained levodopa response of more than 50% with wearing-off, rest tremor, no orthostatic hypotension (systolic fall 14 mmHg), no urinary incontinence, no cerebellar signs, and normal putamina, pons and cerebellum on MRI
Freezing and falls arise after 4 years of levodopa-responsive asymmetric disease; full vertical eye movements, no axial-predominant rigidity, normal midbrain on MRI
No fluctuations of cognition or visual hallucinations; MoCA 24/30 without loss of daily function, and motor onset four years before any cognitive complaint

key_clinical_evidence: Left-onset bradykinesia with decrement, cogwheel rigidity and a 4-5 Hz left-hand rest tremor, and a documented response of more than 50% to levodopa: two supportive criteria with no red flag, clinically established PD [Postuma_2015]
Diary-documented end-of-dose wearing-off about 2.5 hours after each levodopa dose, four OFF periods a day, with OFF-period freezing and two falls at doorways in 3 months, without peak-dose dyskinesia
Prochlorperazine 10 mg up to twice a month for migraine nausea, used since before the PD: a D2 blocker to stop, but not a dose and time course that causes the parkinsonism
TSH 5.8 mIU/L with free T4 0.9 ng/dL on levothyroxine 75 mcg: under-replacement that adds to fatigue and slowing but does not explain the asymmetric rest tremor or the dose-locked fluctuations

sequence_constraints.reason: Exclude structural and vascular causes on MRI before interpreting a DaTscan [Postuma_2015]

alternatives: Ondansetron for migraine-associated nausea (5-HT3 antagonist, no dopamine blockade), unless apomorphine is used
Domperidone 10 mg up to three times daily for the shortest possible time, where available, after an ECG
contraindications: Ondansetron and other 5-HT3 antagonists with apomorphine: contraindicated (profound hypotension and loss of consciousness).

Sumatriptan with MAO-A or non-selective MAO inhibitors: contraindicated (sumatriptan is metabolised by MAO-A). Rasagiline, selegiline and safinamide are selective for MAO-B at recommended doses; selectivity is lost at higher doses.
interactions: Prochlorperazine is a phenothiazine D2 receptor antagonist: even intermittent doses worsen parkinsonism and oppose levodopa. Ondansetron or domperidone (with a QTc check) are alternatives for migraine-associated nausea.
Losartan lowers blood pressure and can add to the orthostatic effect of levodopa.
Omeprazole: reduced gastric acidity can lower levothyroxine absorption; recheck TSH after any change in either drug.
warnings: Prochlorperazine: acute dystonia, akathisia and tardive dyskinesia are additional risks of phenothiazine antiemetics.
Domperidone: QT prolongation; avoid with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors and in cardiac conduction disease.
Sumatriptan and levothyroxine: no clinically relevant interaction with levodopa.
Entacapone: no relevant interaction with her current medicines; it can intensify dopaminergic effects and discolour the urine.

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Rosa Elena Vega is a 58-year-old right-handed Hispanic woman with a 4-year history of Parkinson's disease who presents to the movement disorders clinic accompanied by her husband for evaluation of worsening motor fluctuations and increasingly frequent freezing of gait. She was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease at age 54 following a 12- to 18-month history of progressive left hand rest tremor, left arm stiffness, and generalized slowing. At diagnosis she had an excellent response to levodopa with greater than 50% improvement in motor scores and was titrated to her current regimen of carbidopa-levodopa 25-100 mg four times daily. For approximately the first two years she had excellent motor control throughout the day. However, over the past 18 months she has noticed that the benefit from each levodopa dose seems to wear off approximately 2.5 hours after ingestion. She keeps a symptom diary and consistently notes return of left-hand tremor, bilateral stiffness, bradykinesia, and freezing episodes during these predictable OFF windows. The OFF periods last approximately 30 to 45 minutes until the next dose takes effect. She reports four distinct OFF periods per day, each associated with subjective stiffness, slowing and difficulty initiating movement, and she has two to three freezing-of-gait episodes per week. She has had two actual falls in the past three months, occurring when she froze while walking through doorways. She denies any involuntary writhing movements (dyskinesias) at peak dose. Her husband reports that during OFF periods she is visibly more rigid and speaks more softly, and that her facial expression becomes even more mask-like. She denies any visual hallucinations, significant cognitive complaints beyond occasional word-finding difficulty, or urinary incontinence. She reports long-standing constipation predating her PD diagnosis by approximately five years, managed with fiber supplementation. She also notes hyposmia for at least six to seven years, which she initially attributed to chronic allergies. She has a history of chronic migraine and uses sumatriptan for acute attacks. Approximately twice per month she requires prochlorperazine 10 mg for severe nausea accompanying migraines, a practice that predates her PD diagnosis by several years. Her husband and her neurologist are concerned that the prochlorperazine use could be contributing to worsening Parkinsonian symptoms. Her hypothyroidism was diagnosed three years ago and she is currently taking levothyroxine 75 mcg daily; her most recent TSH was measured six months ago. She denies new medications, recent infections, or other intercurrent illnesses. A maternal history of Parkinson's disease has made her particularly anxious about disease progression.

neurological_exam.additional: Glabellar reflex positive (fails to habituate after 10 taps). Seborrheic dermatitis on scalp and nasolabial folds. Micrographia demonstrated on writing sample — letters progressively smaller and trailing off. No myoclonus. End-of-dose symptom diary reviewed: patient documents return of stiffness, tremor, and freezing approximately 2.5 hours after each levodopa dose, lasting 30-45 minutes prior to next dose ('OFF' periods 4 times daily).
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing intact without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin testing intact bilaterally. Dysdiadochokinesia left hand attributable to bradykinesia. No cerebellar ataxia.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light, 3 mm bilaterally. Visual fields full to confrontation. Extraocular movements full in all directions without nystagmus or supranuclear gaze palsy. Smooth pursuit mildly saccadic. Facial expression markedly hypomimic with reduced spontaneous blink rate (approximately 5 blinks per minute). Mild dysarthria without hypernasality. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline without atrophy or fasciculations. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally.
neurological_exam.gait: Reduced stride length bilaterally with marked reduction of left arm swing; right arm swing mildly reduced. Stooped posture. En bloc turning (requires 5-6 steps to turn 180 degrees). Freezing of gait observed on initiation from standstill and when passing through doorway. Start-hesitation present. Tandem walking impaired. Pull test: two retropulsive steps before recovery. Falls history: two falls in the past three months, both occurring during gait freezing episodes at narrow spaces.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and fully oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) 24/30, losing points on delayed recall (3), verbal fluency (1), the trail-making item (1) and serial subtraction (1). Speech is hypophonic with dysarthric quality but language content intact. Comprehension and repetition preserved. No aphasia or neglect.
neurological_exam.motor: Moderate cogwheel rigidity at the left wrist and left elbow; mild cogwheel rigidity at the right wrist. Marked bradykinesia in the left hand with prominent amplitude decrement and slowing on rapid alternating movements and finger tapping. Right hand bradykinesia is mild. Strength 5/5 in all extremities. No pronator drift. Resting tremor in the left hand, 4-5 Hz, pill-rolling character, intermittent and suppressible with purposeful movement. Subtle re-emergent tremor on left arm extension. No tremor observed in the right hand or lower extremities.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 2+ bilaterally, Achilles 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffmann sign. No clonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, and proprioception intact throughout. Vibration sense mildly diminished at bilateral great toes, age-appropriate.
